q: Typically, what are the inclusions of a set of H-frame scaffolding?
o: 4 pcs H-frames, 2 pcs cross braces and 2 pcs joint pins
2 pcs H-frames, 4 pcs cross braces and 4 pcs joint pins
2 pcs H-frames, 2 pcs cross braces and 4 pcs joint pins
1 pc H-frame, 1 pc cross brace and 2 pcs joint pins
n: A standard set of H-frame scaffolding has 2 H-frames, 2 cross braces to link them into a braced bay, and 4 joint pins to stack frames vertically. Source: OSHS (DOLE) Rule 1414 (Scaffolding); scaffold supplier standard set data.

q: It is the primary cause of punching shear.
n: Punching shear is caused by a concentrated load or reaction, such as a column on a flat slab or footing. It punches a truncated cone through the slab around the load. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 422.6 (Two-way shear); MacGregor & Wight, Reinforced Concrete.

q: What is the common size of wood stakes used in a typical construction layout?
n: Layout stakes are commonly 2 in × 2 in lumber, pointed at one end and driven to set out lines, grades and corners. Source: Max Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (Batter Boards and Stakes); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 1.

q: A metal piece can be hammered, rolled or pressed to produce thin sheets. What property does this metal have?
n: Malleability is a physical property of metals that defines their ability to be hammered, pressed, or rolled into thin sheets without breaking. In other words, it is the property of a metal to deform under compression and take on a new shape. Malleability lets a metal be hammered, rolled or pressed into thin sheets without fracturing. Source: Callister, Materials Science and Engineering; Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 11.

q: What is the usual metal used for framing in a typical curtain wall installation?
n: Although steel-framed curtain walls also exist, aluminum is the most commonly used framing material for curtain walls. | a. Although there is exactly no standard for this, this is the usual specified voltage of many electric fence energizers provided for residential applications. The safe range is actually from 2,000V to 12,000V but some international regulations limit the maximum to 10,000V. Take note that even though the system is high voltage, it is low in current. Aside from this, most electric fences provide pulsating electricity, not a steady flow. Curtain wall mullions and transoms are typically extruded aluminum. It is light, corrosion-resistant and easily extruded into profiles with glazing pockets and thermal breaks. Source: Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 21 (Curtain Walls); AAMA Curtain Wall Manual.

q: Which of the following is the usual range of voltage used for electric fences in residential applications?
n: Residential electric fence energizers deliver short pulses of roughly 7,000–12,000 V. The current is very low, so the shock is a deterrent rather than lethal. Source: IEC 60335-2-76 (Electric Fence Energizers); manufacturer specifications.

q: What component of an electric fence system converts the electric power from the house or from the battery into high voltage pulses?
n: The energizer (fence charger) converts mains or battery power into brief high-voltage pulses sent along the fence wires. Source: IEC 60335-2-76 (Electric Fence Energizers).

q: Electric meters measure what?
n: A kilowatt-hour (energy) meter records the electrical energy consumed over time, in kWh, which is the basis of the utility bill. Source: Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) Part 1, Art. 2.30 (Services – Metering); Stein & Reynolds, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings.

q: Which device can be used to prevent the buildup of mold and mildew growth in a room?
n: Mold and mildew grow when there is excess moisture in the air. Therefore, dehumidifier is the best answer. A dehumidifier removes moisture from the air. Keeping relative humidity below about 60% prevents the growth of mold and mildew. Source: ASHRAE Handbook – Fundamentals (Moisture Management); US EPA, Mold Guide.

q: It is a device used for current limiting.
n: A circuit breaker limits current by automatically opening the circuit on overload or short circuit. Current-limiting breakers also restrict the peak let-through current. Source: Philippine Electrical Code (PEC) Part 1, Art. 2.40 (Overcurrent Protection).

q: In a beam and girder system, which member usually spans the shortest distance?
n: Per the exam key, in a beam-and-girder system the girders run between the columns along the shorter direction and carry the beams. The beams span the longer distance between girders. Code note: which member spans shorter depends on the framing layout. Source: Ching, Building Structures Illustrated (Beam and Girder Systems).

q: Which property of steel allows it to withstand excessive deformations due to high tensile stresses?
n: Ductility is steel's ability to stretch and deform plastically under high tensile stress before fracturing. That gives warning before failure and absorbs seismic energy. Source: NSCP 2015, Ch. 5 (Steel); Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 11.

q: Which differentiates the wide flange beams (W) from the standard I-beams?
o: Standard I-beams have consistent thickness on its webs and flanges
Standard I-beams can have equal or unequal legs
Wide flange beams have sloped inside faces of its flanges
Wide flange beams can be used as beams and columns
n: Standard I-beams are not designed for use as columns. Wide-flange (W) sections have parallel flange faces and proportions efficient in both axes, so they serve as beams and as columns. Standard I-beams (S) have sloped inner flange faces and narrow flanges, so they are used mainly as beams. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, Part 1.

q: In a steel beam-to-column connection, where is the seat angle installed?
o: On the side of the beam web
Above the top flange of the beam
Under the bottom flange of the beam
n: In a seated connection, the seat angle is bolted or welded to the column face under the bottom flange of the beam. The beam rests on it, and a top angle provides stability. Source: AISC Steel Construction Manual, Part 10 (Seated Connections).

q: What does OWSJ mean?
n: OWSJ means Open Web Steel Joist: a light shop-fabricated truss with chords and web bars, used to span floors and roofs. Source: Steel Joist Institute (SJI) Standard Specifications; Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction, Ch. 11.

q: Which of the following parts of a roof truss also act as the tie beam?
n: “Tirante” means bottom chord. In a typical wooden or steel roof truss, the bottom chord also acts as the tie beam. In Filipino carpentry terms, the tirante is the horizontal bottom chord of a roof truss. It ties the feet of the rafters together, acting as the tie beam. Source: Max Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (Roof Framing – local terms).

q: A wall without openings.
n: Although a firewall and a party wall usually don’t have openings, the term “dead wall” is more fitting to the definition mentioned. This term was also in the glossary of the old NBCP. 29 dBA means decibels as adjusted to human ears. A dead wall is a solid wall without doors or windows. Source: Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction (Blank/Dead Wall); 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096 (NBCP), Glossary.

q: What is the usual maximum size of opening for pipe sleeves through an RC beam?
n: A common detailing limit is to keep sleeve openings through an RC beam within about one-fifth of the beam depth, and in the middle third of the depth and span. That limits loss of strength. Source: ACI 318 / NSCP 2015 commentary on beam openings; CRSI Manual of Standard Practice.

q: A structural beam above a door or window opening.
n: A lintel is the beam spanning over a door or window opening. It carries the wall load above the opening. Source: Ching, A Visual Dictionary of Architecture; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 5.

q: A short steel rod or short portion of rebar used to strengthen a joint between abutting concrete members.
n: A dowel is a short bar that crosses a joint between abutting concrete members, such as column to footing or slab panel to slab panel. It transfers shear and holds alignment. Source: ACI 318 / NSCP 2015, Sec. 416 (Dowels); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: It refers to the space between the structural ceiling and the drop ceiling.
n: The plenum is the space between the structural floor or roof above and a suspended ceiling. It is often used for return air and to route ducts and services. Source: Stein & Reynolds, Mechanical and Electrical Equipment for Buildings (Ceiling Plenums); PEC Art. 3.0.

q: What equipment is installed above an opening to maintain internal temperature and air seal between two environments?
n: An air curtain blows a high-velocity air stream down across a doorway. It separates the conditioned interior from outside air, keeping temperature while the door stays open, and keeps out insects and dust. Source: ASHRAE Handbook – HVAC Applications (Air Curtains); AMCA 220.

q: A universal type air conditioner can be installed where?
n: "Universal" (floor/ceiling) split air conditioners are made for flexible mounting: floor-standing, wall-mounted or ceiling-suspended. Source: ASHRAE Handbook – HVAC Systems and Equipment (Ductless Split Systems); manufacturers' installation manuals.

q: In air-conditioner specifications, the noise level in use is measured in
n: Air-conditioner noise is rated in A-weighted decibels (dBA), which follow the ear's sensitivity across frequencies. Source: AHRI Standard 270/275 (Sound Rating of Outdoor Units); Egan, Architectural Acoustics.

q: A cassette type air conditioner is installed where?
n: A cassette-type air conditioner is recessed into the ceiling. It discharges air in two or four directions from a ceiling-flush grille. Source: ASHRAE Handbook – HVAC Systems and Equipment (Ductless Split Systems); manufacturers' installation manuals.

q: Which type of vegetative green roof system has more impact on the structural load of the building?
n: Take note the difference between intensive and extensive vegetative green roof systems. Intensive green roofs have deep soil (about 150 mm to over 1 m), shrubs and trees, and saturated loads of several hundred kg/sqm. Extensive roofs are thin and much lighter. Source: FLL Green Roof Guidelines; Philippine Green Building Code (2015), green roofs.

q: What is the best way to prevent galvanic action in roofing systems?
o: Flashings shall be installed under the roofing sheets
Fastening and roofing accessories shall be made of same metal as the roofing material
Fastening and roofing accessories shall have thermal insulation
n: Galvanic corrosion happens when dissimilar metals touch in the presence of moisture. Making fasteners and accessories of the same metal as the roofing (or a compatible one) prevents it. Source: NRCA Roofing Manual – Metal Panel Systems (Galvanic Compatibility); Allen & Iano, Fundamentals of Building Construction.

q: Reflective glass has what type of coating?
n: Reflective glass has a thin metallic or metal-oxide coating that reflects solar heat and light. Source: GANA Glazing Manual (Reflective/Solar Control Coatings).

q: What is used to seal air leaks around movable building components?
n: Weatherstripping seals the joints around operable parts such as doors and windows. It cuts air leakage and keeps out rain and dust. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 8 (Weatherstripping); ASHRAE Handbook – Fundamentals (Air Leakage).

q: A material used in building envelopes to reduce the flow of thermal energy.
n: Thermal insulation resists heat flow (it has a high R-value) through roofs, walls and floors of the building envelope. Source: ASHRAE Handbook – Fundamentals (Thermal Insulation); Philippine Green Building Code (2015), Envelope.

q: The setting time of concrete starts
o: When concrete achieves 20% of its strength
When placed on its final position
When gravel and cement are mixed
When water is mixed with cement
n: There are two setting times important to concrete, the initial setting time and final setting time. The time is measured from the time when water is mixed with cement which starts the hydration reaction until its substantial hardening. The substantial hardening is measured by 1mm and 5mm needle. Read more about the Vicat needle test for cement or concrete. Take note also of the difference between setting and curing. Setting is the short time hardening of concrete where the concrete becomes rigid enough that you can no longer leave footprints on it. Typical setting time of concrete is 24 to 48 hours. Curing is a longer process where concrete attains its full specified strength. Typical curing time of concrete is usually 28 days. In reality, if the environmental condition allows | continued hydration, concrete increases its strength with years. Setting time is counted from the moment water is added to the cement, when hydration begins. Initial and final set are measured from that point. Source: ASTM C403 / C191 (Time of Setting); Kosmatka et al., Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (PCA).

q: A concrete mix called “PCD” is used where?
n: PCD concrete mix means “pumpcrete design” which means that the concrete design mix is specially designed for pumped concrete. Unlike ordinary design mix, PCD mix is different since it considers the pumpability of concrete mix. Most of the | time, PCD mix has higher design strength than ordinary design mix. A PCD (pumpcrete design) mix is designed for pumping. It has suitable aggregate grading, sand content and slump so it moves through the line without segregating or blocking. Source: ACI 304.2R (Placing Concrete by Pumping Methods).

q: It refers to the installation of construction piles.
n: Pile driving installs prefabricated piles by hammering, vibrating or pressing them into the ground. Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering (Pile Installation); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 3.

q: In ready-mix concrete, samples are ideally obtained from the
n: For truck-mixed concrete, composite samples are taken at regular intervals from the middle portion of the discharge. The first and last parts of the load are not representative. Source: ASTM C172 (Sampling Freshly Mixed Concrete), Sec. 4.1.3.

q: Specified design strength of concrete is generally gained after
n: The specified compressive strength (f'c) is based on cylinders tested at 28 days. Source: NSCP 2015, Sec. 419 / ACI 318 (f'c at 28 days); ASTM C39.

q: It is the craft or trade of joining wooden components in buildings.
n: Although joinery and woodworks may be related, joinery is the more specific term. Take note of the difference between joinery, woodworks and carpentry. 55 1G, 2G, 3G, 4G and 5G represent the five generations of mobile wireless networks where G stands for ‘Generation’. Joinery is the craft of joining wooden members in buildings and furniture: mortise and tenon, dovetail, lap joints and so on. Source: Spence, Carpentry and Building Construction; Harris, Dictionary of Architecture and Construction.

q: Plyboard is ____ than plywood.
n: Plyboard (blockboard) has a core of solid wood strips between veneers. Over long spans it is stiffer and less prone to sagging than plywood of the same thickness. Source: Hoadley, Understanding Wood; Wood Handbook (Panel Products).

q: Low density fiberboard is also known as what?
n: Per the exam key, low-density fiberboard is grouped with chipboard as a low-density wood-fiber or particle panel. Note: in standards, low-density fiberboard is softboard (insulation board), and chipboard is particleboard. Source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook, Ch. 11 (Wood-Based Composites).

q: What type of engineered wood was used for the roof framing of Terminal 2 of the Mactan–Cebu International Airport?
n: Terminal 2 of Mactan–Cebu International Airport is roofed with long-span glue-laminated timber arches. Source: Mactan–Cebu International Airport Authority; Integrated Design Associates (project data).

q: The jack rafter is similar in description to a ____ in stud wall construction.
n: A jack rafter is a shortened rafter, cut short at a hip or valley. In a stud wall the shortened stud above or below an opening is the cripple. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated, Ch. 6–7 (Wood Framing); Spence, Carpentry.

q: ISDN is defined as a set of standards and techniques in telecommunication that enables the digital transmission of data, voice, video, and other services simultaneously across a public telephone network. It means what?
o: Inspection of Service and Digital Norm
n: ISDN means Integrated Services Digital Network. It carries voice, video and data digitally over the public telephone network. Source: ITU-T I-series Recommendations (ISDN).
